query: Accrued unbilled rev. impacts rev. recog. & op. perf.
final_answer: Accrued unbilled revenue arises when revenue is recognized for goods or services delivered but has not yet been billed to customers. This typically happens when the timing of revenue recognition does not match the timing of invoicing. For example, companies may record unbilled revenue as a component of customer receivables based on the estimated amounts of services delivered but not yet billed (see D.pdf, CMI.pdf, TYL.pdf). The impact on revenue recognition is that revenue is recognized in the period when the service is performed or the product is delivered, rather than when the invoice is sent. This ensures that financial statements accurately reflect the company’s performance for that period, even if cash has not yet been collected. Regarding operating performance, recognizing accrued unbilled revenue allows a company’s reported revenues and operating results to better match the underlying business activity, providing a more accurate measure of operational performance. It also results in unbilled receivables being reported as assets on the balance sheet, reflecting the company’s right to payment for work already performed (CMI.pdf, TYL.pdf). In summary, accrued unbilled revenue aligns revenue recognition with actual service delivery or product provision, which improves the accuracy of reported operating performance and financial position.

Key criteria used to assess whether a company is acting as a principal include: - Whether the company is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise to provide the specified goods or service. - Whether the company has inventory risk before the specified good or service has been transferred to the customer. - Whether the company has discretion in establishing the price for the specified good or service. If these factors indicate the company controls the good or service prior to transfer, it is considered the principal and recognizes revenue on a gross basis. If not, the company is considered an agent and recognizes revenue on a net basis, reflecting only the fee or commission it expects to retain (see Chunks 2, 4, and 10). In summary, the assessment focuses on control of the good or service before transfer, responsibility for fulfillment, inventory risk, and pricing discretion.

final_answer: Church & Dwight establishes reserves for consumer and trade promotion liabilities, including coupon redemptions, based on management's best estimates using historical experience and forecasted data. For example, coupon costs are recorded at the time of sale, based on projected redemption rates. If actual coupon redemptions deviate from the estimated rates, this affects the profit and loss (P&L) statement. A higher-than-expected redemption rate would increase the promotional expense, reducing net sales and profit. Conversely, a lower redemption rate would result in lower expenses and higher profit. Regarding cash flow, the impact is indirect. The reserve estimation and recording are non-cash accounting entries at the time of sale. Cash outflows occur when coupons are actually redeemed and paid. If actual redemptions are higher than reserved, future cash outflows increase, and the company will need to recognize additional promotional expense in the P&L for the shortfall. If actual redemptions are lower, there will be a reversal of previously reserved amounts, improving future P&L results and resulting in less cash paid out. In summary, the coupon reserve method directly impacts the P&L through the timing and accuracy of promotional expense recognition, while the cash flow impact arises when the actual redemptions are settled in cash, with variances from estimates leading to adjustments in both future P&L and cash flows.
